objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe, the way an examiner expects on an FOI evaluation, the aviation instructor's responsibilities for adequate instruction, standards of performance and emphasizing the positive; the flight instructor's added duties to evaluate and supervise learners, prepare practical test recommendations and endorsements, and decide when more training and endorsements are required; and the personal characteristics and habits that keep learner frustration low, with an instrument training example for each.
why: The PTS NOTE for Area I tells the evaluator to select at least Tasks E, F and G and one other task, so this Task is tested whenever the FOI are. The AIH says learners look to instructors as role models, so an instructor must project a knowledgeable and professional image, not only know how to teach [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. The FAA places full responsibility for student flight training on the CFI, the cornerstone of aviation safety [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]], and an instructor who endorses someone who does not meet the regulations shows a serious deficiency the FAA may hold that instructor accountable for [[25:184|AIH 9-14]].

warmup: Think first: your instrument learner passed the knowledge test with two subject areas missed and wants you to sign him off for a checkride next week. His last two approaches were sloppy but inside the limits. What exactly are you certifying when you sign, and what would make you say 'not yet'? And how would you tell him so he leaves motivated, not crushed?

key_terms.def: Teaching tailored to the learner: the instructor analyzes the learner's personality, thinking and ability and is ready to change methods as training advances [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].
The established ACS or PTS standards an instructor trains every applicant to, in every task of every area of operation. The ACS/PTS is a testing document, not a teaching document [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].
Conducting instruction so learners get a positive image of aviation; positive instruction results in positive learning [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

Evaluation based on established standards suitably modified for the learner's experience and stage of development, looking at mastery of each element rather than only the overall performance [[25:168|AIH 8-10]].
The flight instructor's guidance and restraint over learners' solo operations, which the AIH calls by far the most important flight instructor responsibility [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
The flight instructor's written recommendation on the airman certificate application. Inspectors and DPEs rely on it as evidence of qualification [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
A logbook or training record entry that marks and formalizes an event such as a privilege granted, an authorization or a limitation incurred [[12:4|AC 61-65K 3]].

At least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training, including a review of part 91 rules and of the maneuvers and procedures the instructor judges necessary [[60:236|14 CFR 61.56(a)]]; a training event, not a practical test [[15:22|AC 61-98E 4.1.1]].
The only way to reestablish instrument currency after failing to meet 61.57(c) for more than six calendar months [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

For a flight instructor: a person who holds a flight instructor certificate, is in compliance with 61.197, and is giving ground or flight training within the privileges and limitations of that certificate. Ground instructors and persons the FAA authorizes can also be authorized instructors [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1(b)]].
Keeping the highest level of knowledge, training and currency, committing to lifelong learning, and behaving in a professional manner [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].

An instructor responsibility met by motivating, keeping learners informed, treating them as individuals, giving credit, criticizing constructively, being consistent and admitting errors [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

chunks.title: Three groups of duties, tested whenever the FOI are

body.p: This Task has three parts. K1 covers duties every aviation instructor has. K2 covers duties added for a flight instructor, such as evaluating learner pilots and deciding when they are ready to solo [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]. K3 covers how a professional instructor looks, talks and treats learners. The CFI lesson FI.I.E teaches the same AIH chapter from the CFI ACS; this lesson follows the PTS wording and adds the CFII's instrument duties. The CFI lesson AI.II.K covers endorsement wording in detail.

**The job in one line.** The job of an aviation instructor is to transfer knowledge. Instructors help learners meet and exceed established standards, measure their performance against those standards and give positive reinforcement along the way [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. Because learners look to instructors as role models, an instructor has to know how to teach and also project a knowledgeable and professional image [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

callout.text: The PTS names the older FAA-H-8083-9 and says 'student'; the 9B says 'learner'. AIH Figure 8-1 lists five responsibilities of all aviation instructors: helping learners learn, providing adequate instruction, demanding appropriate standards of performance, emphasizing the positive and ensuring aviation safety [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. The PTS asks for three of them under K1 and puts minimizing frustration under professionalism.

body.p: The PTS defines 'instructional knowledge' as explanations that follow the teaching procedures of the AIH, and it asks evaluators to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions where possible. So for each item below, keep one instrument training example ready.

check.q: Which three aviation instructor responsibilities does the PTS list under K1, and which two more does AIH Figure 8-1 show?
check.a: Adequate instruction, standards of performance and emphasizing the positive. Figure 8-1 adds helping learners learn and ensuring aviation safety [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

body.p: **Providing adequate instruction** means teaching this learner, not an average one. To tailor your technique you analyze the learner's personality, thinking and ability. No two learners are alike, and one method may not work equally well for all. Talk with the learner at some length about background, interests, temperament and way of thinking, and be ready to change methods as training advances [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. An instructor who analyzes a learner wrongly may find the instruction does not produce the desired results [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

head: What you see
The trap
What the AIH says to do
rows: Quiet, reserved learner who hesitates to act
Deciding this is a slow learner, when the learner understands but lacks self-confidence [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Direct instruction at building self-confidence rather than more drill on fundamentals [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Timid learner
Too much criticism may discourage a timid person, while brisk instruction may push a different learner to work harder [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Match the amount of criticism to the person [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Learner who needs more time
Too much help and encouragement can build a feeling of incompetence [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Use tact, keen perception and delicate handling [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]
Slow progress from discouragement or low confidence
Goals that feel out of reach
Assign more easily attained goals: split a complex task into elements, let the learner get good at each, then raise the difficulty [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]
Fast learner
Makes few mistakes, decides error correction is unimportant, and overconfidence leads to faulty performance [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]
Keep raising the standard each lesson and demand more effort. Never invent deficiencies; unfair criticism destroys confidence in you at once [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]

body.p: The AIH's example of splitting a task is S-turns taught with headings only, then altitude control, drift correction and coordination added one at a time [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

callout.text: Application: the same split works under the hood. A learner discouraged by full holding patterns can first fly only the inbound and outbound legs on headings, then add timing, then wind correction, then the entry. Raise the goal as confidence returns [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

body.p: Adequate instruction is also adequate in the airplane. Flight training is not one size fits all and often must be tailored to the individual, and even after ground school you should review the task with the learner before flight [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. If a learner cannot reach the lesson's proficiency level in the time planned, be ready to schedule additional training [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. A learner may fly a maneuver correctly without understanding it; to check, have the learner vary it slightly, combine it with other operations or apply its elements to other maneuvers [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

In some ways you are a practical psychologist. You meet that duty by knowing the fundamentals of instructing and by careful analysis of, and continuing interest in, each learner [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. Watch one habit in yourself: new instructors tend to teach the way they were taught, or the way they learn best. Having learned that way does not mean it was the best way, so stay open-minded and seek other resources [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

callout.text: Application: a 3,000-hour pilot back for an IPC and a 70-hour private pilot starting the instrument rating need different lessons for the same ILS. Ask about background first, then choose the method [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

check.q: Your instrument learner briefs every approach well but waits for you to call the missed approach. A colleague says 'more drill'. What does the AIH suggest instead?
check.a: A quiet learner may fail to act at the right time from lack of self-confidence even though the situation is understood, so direct instruction at building self-confidence rather than drill on fundamentals [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

body.p: **Establishing standards of performance** means you train each applicant to the established standards in all subject areas, procedures and maneuvers in every task of every area of operation in the appropriate ACS or PTS [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. For your instrument learners that is the Instrument Rating ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8 for airplanes) [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1]].

Standards help learners. Using standards, and measuring performance against them, is key to helping learners: meeting a standard holds its own satisfaction, and people are proud of reaching difficult goals. Making learning easy is not the answer, because learners put more effort into activities that bring rewards [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

bullets: The ACS/PTS is a testing document, not a teaching document [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. Training should focus on learning and understanding why the standards are there and how they were set [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

Do not aim lessons at the minimum acceptable standard for the checkride. Lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed the ACS/PTS before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].
Teach that meeting the standard gives only a limited margin of safety [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].
Certification standards cover the most critical job tasks and do not represent a whole syllabus, so do not limit your objectives to the minimum published requirements [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

A standard describes the desired knowledge, behavior or skill in specific terms, with conditions and criteria. When a learner performs to well-defined standards, evidence of learning is apparent [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].
Partway through training, evaluate against the established standards suitably modified for the learner's experience and stage of development [[25:168|AIH 8-10]].

callout.text: Application: the CFII PTS you test under allows no more than a ¾-scale deflection of the vertical or lateral guidance on final. That is a test limit, not a lesson goal. Build early approach lessons around flying the needles near center, and explain why a limit exists at all [[25:171|AIH 9-1]] [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

body.p: The PHAK makes the same point from the learner's side: practical tests are a sampling of pilot ability compressed into a short time, and the instructor's goal is to train the 'total' pilot [[1:39|PHAK 1-24]].

callout.text: Train beyond the ACS; test to it. The ACS is the finish line, not the lesson plan [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

check.q: An instrument learner asks, 'What is the least I can get away with on the ILS?' How do you answer as the AIH would?
check.a: The ACS is a testing document, not a teaching document. Meeting the standard gives only a limited margin of safety, and lesson standards should reach or exceed the ACS before checkride preparation [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:163|AIH 8-5]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

body.p: **Emphasizing the positive** starts with you. The way you conduct yourself and the attitudes you show make an impression, and teaching so that learners get a positive image of aviation adds to your success [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

The reason is the learning process. A negative self-concept inhibits perception, fear hurts perception, feeling threatened limits it, and negative motivation is weaker than positive motivation. Knowing this is not enough: you have to detect these feelings in learners and keep them from undermining instruction [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

head: First lesson
What the learner takes away
rows: Built on fear (AIH example)

Preflight taught as a guard against disastrous emergencies, taxiing as a way to lose control, stalls as 'how so many people lose their lives', forced landings on day one. The learner may wonder if learning to fly is a good idea [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]
Built positively (AIH example)

Preflight to get acquainted with the aircraft, then a perfectly normal flight to a nearby airport and back. Afterward, point out how easy the trip was and that nothing critical happened or was expected [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]

body.p: This does not drop stalls and emergencies from training. Introduce them after the learner knows normal operations, using a syllabus that builds a foundation, so they are less discouraging and do not block learning through fear [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]. Treat fears as a normal reaction rather than ignoring them, and present safe flying practices as the way to satisfying, efficient, uninterrupted flights, not only as a way to prevent catastrophe [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

Positive does not mean silent about errors. The law of effect says satisfying outcomes tend to be repeated, so create situations that promote success [[25:63|AIH 3-12]], and comment on progress before discussing what needs improving [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]. When you point out areas to improve, give concrete suggestions and, if possible, avoid ending the evaluation on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

callout.text: Nothing in aviation demands that learners suffer. A learner's failure to perform often comes from the instructor's inability to transfer the information. Positive instruction results in positive learning [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

Application: do not open an instrument course with partial-panel unusual attitudes 'to build respect'. Start with attitude flying the learner can master, then bring in failures and emergencies once normal hood work is familiar [[25:161|AIH 8-3]] [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

check.q: Your new instrument learner arrives nervous after hearing a friend's IMC horror story. How do you build the first lesson?
check.a: Treat the fear as a normal reaction [[25:45|AIH 2-12]] and build a lesson she can succeed at: normal attitude flying first, emergencies once normal operations are familiar [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]. Comment on her progress before what needs work [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

chunks.title: Flight instructor responsibilities: what is added

body.p: **Flight instructor responsibilities** are added to the K1 duties. All aviation instructors carry an enormous responsibility because their learners will ultimately be flying, servicing or repairing aircraft. Learning to fly should be a habit-building period, and the flight instructor's job is to 'mold' the learner into a safe pilot who takes a professional approach to flying. Flight instructors may also have to evaluate learners and decide when they are ready to solo. More of these duties are in 14 CFR part 61 and FAA advisory circulars [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

Figure 8-5 lists eight added duties [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]. The PTS asks about three groups of them: evaluation and supervision (K2a), practical test recommendations and endorsements (K2b), and additional training and endorsement requirements (K2c). The next six chunks take them in that order.

bullets: The FAA places full responsibility for student flight training on the CFI, the cornerstone of aviation safety [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]]. AC 61-98E adds that flight instructors bear a responsibility to produce and sustain the safest pilots possible [[15:19|AC 61-98E 2.4]].
Stay current and proficient in the aircraft you use, and encourage each pilot to keep 'raising the bar' [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

Do not ignore or ridicule physiological obstacles such as unfamiliar noise, G sensations or an uneasy stomach; explain their causes. A sick learner may not have the capacity to learn [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

Give adequate flight and ground instruction on each ACS/PTS item, including special emphasis items such as positive exchange of flight controls, collision avoidance, CFIT, ADM and risk management, checklist usage and spatial disorientation [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].
Keep a current library and follow procedures the way the FAA prescribes. When you need help, ask a more experienced instructor, a DPE or the local FSDO [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

callout.text: To give instrument training for an instrument rating, you must hold an instrument rating appropriate to the aircraft on your flight instructor certificate [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]]. Of the 40 hours of instrument time an instrument-airplane applicant logs, 15 must come from an authorized instructor who holds an instrument-airplane rating [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)]].

check.q: A CFI who holds only airplane single-engine on her instructor certificate offers to finish your learner's instrument rating training. Can she?
check.a: Not for the instrument rating. Instrument training for its issuance requires an instrument rating appropriate to the aircraft on the flight instructor certificate [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]].

chunks.title: Student pilot evaluation: judging demonstrated ability

body.p: **Providing student pilot evaluation** means judging a learner's ability to perform a maneuver or procedure [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]. Evaluation of demonstrated ability rests on established standards of performance, suitably modified for the learner's experience and stage of development, and it looks at mastery of each element of the maneuver rather than merely the overall performance [[25:168|AIH 8-10]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Qualification for solo and solo cross-country depends on these demonstrations [[25:168|AIH 8-10]].

**Keep the learner informed.** Report progress as each maneuver is completed or in the postflight critique, and use written notes so you cover everything you saw. When you explain errors, point out the elements where the deficiencies began and suggest corrections [[25:168|AIH 8-10]]. Traditional grading scales such as 'excellent, good, fair, poor' often meet the instructor's needs but not the learner's; after a scenario, use collaborative assessment: the learner's self-assessment, then a discussion comparing it with yours [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

bullets: Flight instructors generally use the review, collaborative assessment, written tests and performance-based tests [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
An assessment can also be a tool for reteaching: demonstrate the maneuver, let the learner practice under direction, then evaluate by watching the performance [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
Safety permitting, let learners progress part of the way into a mistake and find the way out; learners who seldom correct an error have trouble learning the maneuver [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
Verify that learners meet the proficiency requirements before you send them to any stage check [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

body.p: **Before solo.** The learner must show consistency in the solo tasks: takeoffs and landings, keeping aircraft control as the priority, proficiency in flight, traffic pattern operation, navigation and radio skills, and knowing to ask ATC for help. Mastery means consistent use and increasing accuracy, and readiness is generally decided when you watch the learner perform consistently from preflight to shutdown without your help [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

callout.text: Application for the CFII: your instrument learners are already pilots, but the rule is the same. Judge each element of an approach (briefing, setup, course and glidepath, callouts, the missed approach decision) against the standard for that stage of training, not just whether the airplane reached the runway [[25:168|AIH 8-10]].

If you believe a learner may have a serious psychological abnormality, refrain from instructing that learner and have an instructor who does not know the learner fly an evaluation flight; the two of you then confer. If, after that consultation, you believe the learner may have a serious psychological deficiency, withhold solo endorsements and practical test recommendations [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

check.q: Your learner flew the RNAV approach within limits, but only after you set up the approach she forgot to load. What does evaluation by elements tell you?
check.a: Evaluation looks at mastery of the elements, not merely the overall performance [[25:168|AIH 8-10]]. The setup element is not yet mastered, so debrief it and practice it before you call the approach done.

chunks.title: Student pilot supervision: guidance and restraint

body.p: **Providing student pilot supervision.** Flight instructors provide guidance and restraint for their learners' solo operations. The AIH calls this by far the most important flight instructor responsibility. You are the only person in a position to decide a learner is ready for solo, and before endorsing solo you should require consistent ability on all the fundamental maneuvers [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

head: Supervision on paper
What the rule requires
rows: Solo endorsement
Only after you gave the required training and decided the student can fly safely under known circumstances, subject to any limitations you consider necessary [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)(1)]]
Make and model, 90 days

A student may solo only with an endorsement for the specific make and model from an authorized instructor who gave the training within the 90 days before the flight [[60:277|14 CFR 61.87(n)]]. It stays current only if an authorized instructor updates it every 90 days [[60:278|14 CFR 61.87(p)(4)]]
Solo cross-country
Only after you find the student's preparation, planning, equipment and procedures adequate for that flight under the existing conditions [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)(2)]]
Class B
Only after ground and flight training in that Class B airspace or at that airport, and a finding of proficiency [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)(3)]]

body.p: Supervision with you aboard:

bullets: Guard the controls. When needed, take them and calmly announce 'I have the flight controls.' Anxious learners can be incredibly strong, and nothing is gained by fighting them for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Never let learners exceed your limits, and do not exceed your own ability to perceive a problem, decide and react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Judge how much control to use: be ready to take over on hazardous or difficult maneuvers, especially first attempts, but avoid needless interruptions when progress is normal [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

See and avoid: if learners think you do all the scanning, they never build the habit. In one midair collision study, flight instructors were on board in 37 percent of the accidents [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

body.p: First solo: be present to answer questions, pick a time of day with traffic, wind and sun angle in mind, carry a portable radio if possible, keep calls to a minimum and never talk to the learner on short final. Debrief right after the flight while it is vivid [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Require full stop landings on the first solo, which gives you the chance to stop the flight if needed [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

callout.text: Application for the CFII: under the hood your learner cannot see traffic, so the outside scan is yours. AC 61-98E says that when a check is flown with a view-limiting device it is the flight instructor's responsibility to stay vigilant for other aircraft throughout the flight [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.1]]. Say so in the briefing, along with the exchange of controls.

check.q: Your student pilot's solo endorsement for the C172 is 95 days old, and the airplane is free this afternoon. What is the rule?
check.a: She may not solo: the make and model endorsement must come from an authorized instructor who gave the training within the 90 days before the flight [[60:277|14 CFR 61.87(n)]]. Fly with her and update it [[60:278|14 CFR 61.87(p)(4)]].

body.p: **Preparing practical test recommendations.** The airman certificate application has a block for the written recommendation of the flight instructor who prepared the applicant. Signing it is a serious responsibility: require the applicant to thoroughly demonstrate the knowledge and skill for the certificate or rating, and never less than the complete procedure in the applicable ACS/PTS [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

FAA inspectors and DPEs rely on your recommendation as evidence of qualification, as proof that you reviewed the subject areas missed on the knowledge test, and as assurance that the applicant was thoroughly briefed on the ACS/PTS [[25:183|AIH 9-13]] [[25:203|AIH C-2]]. If you trained and prepared the applicant competently, the applicant should have no problem passing [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

callout.text: To take a practical test the applicant needs, if part 61 requires it, an endorsement certifying training received and logged within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application, that the applicant is prepared for the test, and that the applicant has shown satisfactory knowledge of the subject areas missed on the knowledge test [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)]]. The knowledge test must have been passed within the 24-calendar-month period preceding the month the practical test is completed [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(1)]].

body.p: **The instrument rating set.** For an instrument applicant you sign A.42 for the knowledge test, A.43 for the practical test and A.44, the instrument version of the 61.39 prerequisites [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.42]]. The rule behind A.43 requires an endorsement certifying the applicant is prepared for the practical test [[60:250|14 CFR 61.65(a)(6)]], and the experience must include 3 hours of instrument flight training from an authorized instructor in an appropriate airplane within 2 calendar months before the date of the practical test [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]].

**Retests.** After a Notice of Disapproval, the applicant needs another endorsement that the training was received and the applicant is prepared, plus your recommendation on the 8710 for each retest [[12:11|AC 61-65K 14.2]]. The rule requires the necessary training from an authorized instructor who found the applicant proficient, and an endorsement from the instructor who gave it [[60:227|14 CFR 61.49(a)]]. After a Letter of Discontinuance no additional endorsement is needed, and credit for passed areas lasts 60 calendar days [[12:11|AC 61-65K 14.3]].

callout.text: Have applicants use IACRA whenever possible. It checks entries internally and reduces errors, while a mistake on a paper form can significantly delay the certificate [[25:203|AIH C-2]].

check.q: Your instrument applicant will apply in June. His last lesson with you was in March, and since then he has only practiced alone in the school's AATD. Can you sign A.44 today?
check.a: No. The training you certify must be logged within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application, here April or May [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)]], and he needs 3 hours of instrument flight training from an authorized instructor in an airplane within 2 calendar months before the test date [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]]. Practice alone is not training time [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(h)(1)]]. Fly with him first.

chunks.title: Endorsements and records that hold up

body.p: **Endorsements.** Part 61 gives you the authority. Within the limitations of your instructor certificate and ratings, you may give training, conduct certain checking events and issue endorsements related to student pilot, pilot, flight instructor and ground instructor certificates, aircraft and instrument ratings, flight reviews, operating privileges, recency, and practical and knowledge tests [[60:345|14 CFR 61.193(a)]]. An endorsement marks and formalizes an event such as a privilege granted or a limitation incurred, and using the recommended endorsements reduces the risk that someone acts without a prerequisite or misunderstands a limitation [[12:4|AC 61-65K 3]].

bullets: Make it legible, with your signature, the date you signed, your CFI certificate number, and your RE end date or certificate expiration date, as applicable, for example /s/ [date] J. J. Jones 987654321CFI RE 12-31-2026 [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]].

Wording need not match the AC exactly, and you may customize it for special circumstances, but at a minimum cite the part 61 section completed [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. Word it as closely as possible to AC 61-65 [[25:202|AIH C-1]].
No rule prevents you from adding a requirement to an endorsement [[25:202|AIH C-1]].
Never endorse yourself for any certificate, rating, flight review, authorization, operating privilege, practical test or knowledge test [[60:349|14 CFR 61.195(i)]].
Training entries need a description of the training, the lesson length, and your signature, certificate number and expiration or RE end date [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]].

callout.text: Sign the logbook of everyone you give flight or ground training. Keep a record of each person you endorsed for solo (with the date) and each person you endorsed for a knowledge or practical test (with the kind of test, date and result), for at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]].

If you fail to make sure a learner or an additional-rating pilot meets the regulations before endorsing solo or a rating, that is a serious deficiency in performance, the FAA may hold you accountable, and it is a breach of faith with the learner [[25:184|AIH 9-14]].

body.p: Using AC 61-65 keeps you from omitting a required endorsement and ensures standardization [[25:202|AIH C-1]]. AC 61-65K itself is guidance whose content is not legally binding in its own right; the requirements are in part 61 [[12:4|AC 61-65K 1]].

check.q: A new CFII writes an IPC endorsement with her signature and the date, but no certificate number or RE end date. What is missing according to AC 61-65K?
check.a: Each endorsement must include the instructor's signature, date of signature, CFI certificate number, and RE end date or certificate expiration date, as applicable [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]].

chunks.title: Additional training: what the rule requires, what the pilot needs

body.p: **Determining requirements for additional training and endorsements.** Flight instructors also train and endorse pilots who are already certificated: flight reviews, instrument proficiency checks, and the additional training for high-performance, high-altitude and tailwheel airplanes, among others [[25:202|AIH C-1]]. AC 61-98 gives guidance for flight reviews and recent flight experience [[25:204|AIH C-3]]. The job has two steps: decide what the rules require, then decide what this pilot actually needs, which is often more.

head: Situation
Requirement
Sample endorsement
rows: Acting as PIC

A flight review since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month of the flight [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]: at least 1 hour of flight and 1 hour of ground training, part 91 rules plus maneuvers at your discretion [[60:236|14 CFR 61.56(a)]]
Instrument currency lapsed more than six calendar months
First time as PIC of a complex airplane
Ground and flight training, found proficient, one-time endorsement [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(e)]]
First time as PIC of a high-performance airplane (an engine of more than 200 horsepower)
Ground and flight training, found proficient, one-time endorsement [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]]
Retest after a failed knowledge or practical test
Additional training, and an endorsement from the instructor who gave it [[60:227|14 CFR 61.49(a)]]

body.p: **Flight reviews.** A flight review is a training event in which proficiency is evaluated, not a practical test. It may take more than the 1 plus 1 hour minimum, and the instructor decides the total time [[15:22|AC 61-98E 4.1.1]]. Interview the pilot about the flying they do [[15:23|AC 61-98E 4.2]], read the logbook for total time, time in type and recency [[15:25|AC 61-98E 4.2.3]], and agree on how the review will run and what counts as satisfactory [[15:25|AC 61-98E 4.2.4]]. The objectives should include a thorough checkout for the certificate and ratings held, with standards at least those for issuing that certificate [[25:204|AIH C-3]]. You may not endorse a flight review unless you conducted it under 61.56(a) [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(d)(5)]].

callout.text: If a review is not satisfactory, log it as 'dual instruction given', not as a failure, use the ACS or PTS to discuss what needs work, and recommend additional training [[15:28|AC 61-98E 4.4.1]] [[15:29|AC 61-98E 4.4.1]]. No logbook entry showing unsatisfactory performance is required [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.69]].

body.p: **Checkouts.** An instructor who checks out a pilot in an aircraft that needs no type rating accepts major responsibility for the safety of future passengers. Be fully qualified in the aircraft, use a plan of action and a written syllabus based on the ACS/PTS, and record the exact extent of the checkout in the pilot's logbook, which protects both of you. If performance is not good enough to sign off, debrief every problem area and schedule more training, or refer the pilot to another instructor [[25:205|AIH C-4]]. The FAA recommends a comprehensive checkout in each make and model, because accident rates rise for pilots with little or no time in the type flown [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]].

callout.text: Application: be honest about your own limits. AC 61-98E says that if you are not proficient in an aircraft or a specialized field of instruction, such as transition training in a particular technically advanced aircraft, you should decline and help the pilot find a qualified instructor [[15:19|AC 61-98E 2.4.1]].

check.q: A pilot asks you for a flight review in a light twin. You hold only single-engine ratings on your CFI certificate. What do you do?
check.a: Decline. To give a flight review in a multiengine airplane, the instructor must hold an airplane multiengine rating on both the pilot and flight instructor certificates [[15:25|AC 61-98E 4.2.5]]. Help the pilot find a qualified instructor [[15:19|AC 61-98E 2.4.1]].

chunks.title: Instrument recency and the IPC: the CFII's additional training

body.p: For a CFII, additional training includes instrument recency and the IPC. To act as PIC under IFR or in weather below VFR minimums, a pilot must have performed and logged, within the 6 calendar months preceding the month of the flight, at least six instrument approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking courses with navigation systems, in actual or simulated conditions [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]. A full flight simulator, flight training device or aviation training device may be used, in any combination with an aircraft [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(2)]].

A pilot who has not met those requirements for more than six calendar months can reestablish currency only with an instrument proficiency check, which must include the areas of operation in the applicable instrument rating ACS [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]. An IPC may be given by an examiner, an authorized instructor, and certain company check pilots, military evaluators and persons the FAA approves [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(3)]].

callout.text: To conduct an IPC, the flight instructor must hold an instrument rating on both the pilot certificate and the flight instructor certificate, appropriate to the category and class of aircraft used [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]]. You may not endorse a logbook for an IPC unless you tested the pilot under 61.57(d) [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(d)(6)]].

bullets: Tailor the IPC to the pilot, as with a flight review [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.3]]. Discuss the conditions, and use a plan of action with realistic scenarios to organize the tasks [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.3]].
Agree beforehand on how it will run and what counts as satisfactory [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.4]].
Knowledge portion: part 91, charts and procedures, weather, preflight planning, systems and instruments, airworthiness for IFR and ATC procedures [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]] [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]].
Skill portion: the tasks in the instrument rating ACS task table, plus anything else you need to see, and the pilot must show satisfactory basic attitude instrument flying [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.3]].

All or part may be done in an FFS, FTD or ATD as the ACS allows, but only an advanced ATD (AATD) may be used for the IPC; check the device's letter of authorization [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.2]]. The rule's own list names an aircraft, an FFS or an FTD [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(2)]], so read the LOA before you plan ATD time.
Whatever the result, debrief with a comprehensive analysis and suggestions for weak areas [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.4]] [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4]].

callout.text: Do not endorse an unsatisfactory IPC; log the session as 'dual instruction given' [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]]. No logbook entry showing unsatisfactory performance is required [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]].

body.p: Who may teach which instrument skills is also part of determining requirements. A CFI with the category and class rating may give flight training on control and maneuvering an airplane solely by reference to the instruments [[60:350|14 CFR 61.195(l)(1)]], but instrument training for an instrument rating needs the instrument rating on the instructor certificate [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]].

callout.text: Application: legal is not the same as sharp. Meeting a standard gives only a limited margin of safety [[25:163|AIH 8-5]], so end every IPC by talking about a plan to stay proficient, not just current.

check.q: A pilot last logged instrument approaches two years ago and asks you to ride along while he flies six approaches to get current. What is required?
check.a: He has failed to meet 61.57(c) for more than six calendar months, so only an IPC reestablishes currency [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]. You may give it if you hold instrument ratings on both your pilot and instructor certificates [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]].

body.p: **Professionalism.** The aviation instructor is the central figure in aviation training and is responsible for all phases of required training. Professionals keep the highest level of knowledge, training and currency, commit to lifelong learning through study, service and membership in organizations such as SAFE and NAFI, and build a library of current resources. Being a professional also means behaving in a professional manner [[25:165|AIH 8-7]].
**Important personal characteristics**, under the AIH's own headings [[25:166|AIH 8-8]] [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]:

head: Characteristic
What it looks like
What breaks it
rows: Sincerity
Straightforward and honest at all times [[25:166|AIH 8-8]]
Hiding inadequacy behind a smokescreen of unrelated instruction, or any facade of pretentiousness; the learner loses respect and confidence [[25:166|AIH 8-8]]
Acceptance of the learner

Accept learners as they are, faults and problems included; both of you work toward the same objective [[25:166|AIH 8-8]]. Acceptance rather than ridicule, support rather than reproof [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]
Anything that implies degrading the learner. Criticizing a slow learner is like a doctor reprimanding a patient for not getting well fast enough [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]
Personal appearance and habits
Neat, clean, appropriately dressed; common courtesy is perhaps the most important habit [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]
Rudeness, thoughtlessness or inattention; even body odor or bad breath distracts in close quarters [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]
Demeanor
Calm, thoughtful and disciplined, showing competence and genuine interest in the learner's well-being [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]

Erratic movements, distracting speech habits, mood swings, contradictory directions, reacting differently to the same error, unreasonable demands, unfair criticism, an overbearing or flippant manner [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]
Proper language
Speak normally, positively and descriptively [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]
Profanity and obscene language, which lead to distrust or at best a lack of full confidence [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]

body.p: **Safety by example.** Learners see you as a role model and imitate your habits, consciously or not, so your safety talk means little if you do not demonstrate it consistently [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]. Students watch your flying habits during lessons and when you fly for yourself [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]].

**Qualifications and growth.** Know the function and proper use of every instrument, avionics unit and system you teach with; the wide variety of GPS and glass displays makes this especially important [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]. Keep up with current techniques and requirements, because continued use of outmoded procedures or obsolete requirements usually involves rationalization [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]. Successful instructors do not become complacent with their own qualifications [[25:168|AIH 8-10]].

callout.text: Application: sincerity in the instrument airplane. When a learner asks about a GPS mode you are not sure of, say so, find the answer in the guide together, and show how you check it. Bluffing is the smokescreen the AIH warns about, and learners sense it quickly [[25:166|AIH 8-8]] [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

check.q: Your learner busts an altitude by 200 feet for the second lesson in a row. Last week you laughed it off; today you snap at him. Which characteristic slipped?
check.a: Demeanor: the AIH says to avoid reacting differently to similar errors at different times and to keep a calm, disciplined manner [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]. It also breaks 'be consistent' [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

body.p: **Minimizing student frustration** in the classroom or the airplane is the instructor's responsibility [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Lesson plans in an organized curriculum help learners measure their progress. Most pilots do not want to be learners, so being able to 'see an end in sight' reduces frustration and raises motivation [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

head: Method
Why it works
Instrument example (Application)
rows: Motivate learners
More is gained from wanting to learn than from being forced. When learners see the benefit and purpose of a lesson, enjoyment and effort go up [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Tie the holding lesson to the busy airports the learner flies into
Keep learners informed
Learners feel insecure when they do not know what is expected or what will happen. Give a course overview, progress updates and notice of exams and assignments [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Show where today's partial-panel lesson sits in the syllabus and when the stage check comes
Approach learners as individuals
Teaching only to the group aims at an average personality that fits no one [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
In an instrument ground school, learn each learner's background before you assign approach briefings
Give credit when due
Unnoticed good work frustrates. Deserved praise pays dividends, but praise given too freely becomes valueless [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Name the specific good thing: 'Your level-off at the MDA was right on'
Criticize constructively
'Unsatisfactory' with no explanation frustrates, and errors not identified are perpetuated through faulty practice. Brief the error and how to correct it [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
'You chased the glideslope with big pitch changes; try one degree at a time'
Be consistent
Learners want to please you; if the same thing is fine one day and wrong the next, they are confused [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Hold the same approach standard every lesson, not only on strict days
Admit errors
Learners sense a cover-up or bluff quickly, and it destroys confidence. If in doubt, admit it [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
'I gave you the wrong frequency. My mistake. Here is the right one.'

body.p: Other sources of frustration the AIH names, with the fix: learning plateaus, met first by explaining that learning seldom moves at a constant pace [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]; skills taught simple to complex, so the learner gains confidence and is less likely to become frustrated [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]; and a struggling learner, whom you can move back to a block they do well, as in the AIH example of reviewing slow flight with a learner who is having trouble with landings [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Clear objectives give the big picture, which can relieve a significant source of uncertainty and frustration [[25:110|AIH 5-7]], and discouragement is rare when learners feel nothing is being withheld from them or neglected in their training [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

callout.text: The seven rules in Figure 8-4 order: Motivate, Keep informed, Approach as individuals, Give credit, Criticize constructively, Be consistent, Admit errors [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

Impossible or unreasonable goals discourage the learner, reduce effort and slow learning [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]. Impatience can also come from instruction paced for a slow learner being given to a motivated fast one [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

check.q: Your learner grumbles that he never knows what the next lesson is or how close he is to the checkride. Which method fixes this, and how?
check.a: Keep learners informed: give a course overview, keep them posted on progress and give adequate notice of exams [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Seeing an end in sight reduces frustration [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

chunks.title: Risks, common instructor errors and how this Task is tested

body.p: The PTS asks the evaluator to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions where possible, so expect 'what would you do' more than definitions. It also lists knowledge of the flight instructor's responsibilities for the certification process, logbook entries and endorsements among the items for a satisfactory practical test. The table shows instructor errors the sources warn about.

head: Instructor error
What can follow
The fix
rows: Training only to pass the test
Many accidents come from training aimed at passing the tests while risk management is ignored [[30:4|RMH ii]]
Teach why the standards exist, and set lesson standards at or above the ACS [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]
Signing a recommendation on a hunch
A serious deficiency the FAA may hold you accountable for, and a breach of faith with the learner [[25:184|AIH 9-14]]
Require the complete ACS/PTS procedure first [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]
Logging an unsatisfactory flight review or IPC as a failure
Treats a training event as a test [[15:22|AC 61-98E 4.1.1]]
Log dual instruction given and recommend training [[15:28|AC 61-98E 4.4.1]] [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]]
Giving an IPC without the instrument rating on your CFI certificate
A check outside the instructor requirements [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]]
Hold the instrument rating on both certificates [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]]
Teaching in an aircraft or avionics you do not know
You fall short of the thorough familiarity with every instrument, avionics unit and system the AIH expects, which matters more with today's variety of GPS and glass displays [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]
Decline, or get qualified first [[15:19|AC 61-98E 2.4.1]]
Vague or unfair criticism
Destroys the learner's confidence in you, and unidentified errors are perpetuated [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Name the error and the fix [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Letting the learner rely on you to scan
The learner never develops constant vigilance [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Correct at once any maneuver entered without a clearing check [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]

callout.text: The flight instructor's primary legal responsibility concerns the decision whether to endorse a learner for solo or to recommend a practical test leading to certification [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

body.p: How to answer in the oral: name the element in the PTS words, give the AIH idea in one sentence, cite the rule if there is one, then give an instrument training example. For K2b, be ready to write A.1, A.2 and A.42 to A.44 on paper [[12:40|AC 61-65K A.1]] [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.44]].

check.q: An examiner asks, 'What is your primary legal responsibility as a flight instructor?' What do you say?
check.a: The decision whether to endorse a learner for solo or to recommend a practical test [[25:49|AIH 2-16]], made only after the learner has demonstrated the complete ACS/PTS procedure [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

scenario.title: A month on the CFII schedule
scenario.setup: You are a CFII at a busy part 61 school. Sam, an instrument learner with 42 hours of instrument time, passed his knowledge test with two subject areas missed and wants a checkride on the 28th of this month. His last airplane lesson with you was four months ago; since then he has practiced alone in the school's AATD. Priya, a quiet instrument learner, flies good approaches but waits for you to call the missed approach. Ken, an instrument-rated owner who last flew instrument approaches two years ago, asks for an IPC in his new glass-panel airplane, a model you have never flown. And at the end of a long day you notice you snapped at a learner for the same altitude error you laughed off last week.

questions.q: Sam wants you to sign him off today. What must be true before you sign A.43 and A.44, and what is missing?
questions.a: The 61.39 endorsement certifies training logged within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application, readiness, and review of the missed subject areas [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)]]. The instrument rule also needs 3 hours of instrument flight training from an authorized instructor in an airplane within 2 calendar months before the test date [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]]. Training time is logged only when training is received from an authorized instructor [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(h)(1)]], so solo AATD practice gives neither. Fly with him, review the two missed areas, and require the complete ACS procedure before you sign [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

questions.q: Sam pushes back: 'Just get me to the ACS limits, nothing more.' How do you answer?
questions.a: The ACS is a testing document, not a teaching document, and meeting the standard gives only a limited margin of safety [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]. Lesson standards should reach or exceed the ACS before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. Tie it to his own goal of flying real IFR trips, which motivates rather than lectures [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

questions.q: How do you handle Priya, and what is the trap?
questions.a: The trap is calling her slow. A quiet, reserved learner may understand the situation but fail to act from lack of self-confidence, so aim at confidence rather than more drill [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. Safety permitting, let her make the missed approach decision herself [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], and give credit when she does [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

questions.q: What does Ken need, and should you be the one to give it?
questions.a: Two years without approaches is more than six calendar months, so only an IPC restores currency [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]. You hold the instrument ratings the IPC requires [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]], but you have never flown his airplane. Get qualified in it first, or decline and help him find an instructor who is [[15:19|AC 61-98E 2.4.1]].

questions.q: Ken's IPC goes poorly on partial panel. What do you write and say?
questions.a: Do not endorse it; log the session as 'dual instruction given' [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.1]], and no unsatisfactory entry is required [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.71]]. Give a comprehensive analysis with suggestions for the weak areas [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.4]], briefing each error and how to correct it [[25:162|AIH 8-4]], and plan the next lesson.

questions.q: You snapped at a learner for an error you laughed off last week. What did that break, and what now?
questions.a: Demeanor, which avoids reacting differently to similar errors at different times [[25:167|AIH 8-9]], and the rule to be consistent [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Admit the error honestly; learners respect it, and a bluff destroys confidence [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Then brief the altitude error and its fix calmly.

skills.do: Explain aloud, as you would to an examiner, how you decide to sign a practical test recommendation for an instrument applicant: what 61.39(a)(6) certifies, the A.42 to A.44 set, the 3 hours in 2 calendar months, why you require the complete ACS procedure first, and what you keep in your own records.
skills.practice: On a blank logbook page, write A.42, A.43 and A.44 for a made-up instrument applicant, and A.1 and A.2 for a made-up private applicant, each with a full signature block [[12:40|AC 61-65K A-7]] [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.43]]. Then have a study partner play an applicant who is missing one requirement and see whether you catch it [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)]] [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]].

skills.do: Describe the seven methods to minimize student frustration in Figure 8-4 order, each with an instrument training example, and connect them to the personal characteristics on the Instructor Do's list.
skills.practice: Debrief a friend's practice approach in a training device using all seven methods, then ask the friend which ones they noticed and which they missed [[25:162|AIH 8-4]] [[25:166|AIH 8-8]].

quiz.q: Your quiet instrument learner understands the approach but waits for you to call the missed approach. Per the AIH, what should your instruction aim at?
options: More drill on approach fundamentals
Building his self-confidence
Firmer criticism to speed him up
A faster syllabus to push him
quiz.why: A quiet, reserved learner may fail to act at the right time from lack of self-confidence even though the situation is understood, so direct instruction at building self-confidence rather than drill on fundamentals [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. Too much criticism discourages a timid person [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

quiz.q: A fast learner flies near-perfect holds and has started brushing off small errors. What does the AIH recommend?
options: Invent a few faults to humble him
Let it go, since he meets the ACS
Raise the standard each lesson
Pair him with a slow learner
quiz.why: For fast learners, constantly raise the standard of performance for each lesson and demand greater effort. Never invent deficiencies; unfair criticism destroys confidence in the instructor [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

quiz.q: How does the AIH describe the ACS/PTS?
options: A complete syllabus for each certificate
The goal for every lesson
A guide used only by examiners
A testing document, not a teaching one
quiz.why: The ACS/PTS is a testing document, not a teaching document [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. Certification tests cover the most critical tasks and do not represent an entire syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

quiz.q: Which first instrument lesson best emphasizes the positive?
options: Normal attitude flying she can master
Partial-panel unusual attitudes, to build respect
A full briefing on IMC accident statistics
A hard ILS in turbulence
quiz.why: Introduce emergencies after the learner knows normal operations, so they do not discourage or block learning through fear [[25:161|AIH 8-3]]. The law of effect says to create situations that promote success [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

quiz.q: On what does the AIH base the evaluation of a learner's demonstrated ability?
options: The overall result of the maneuver
Stage-adjusted standards, element by element
The instructor's general feel for the learner
How the learner compares with classmates
quiz.why: Evaluation of demonstrated ability is based on established standards suitably modified to the learner's experience and stage of development, and considers mastery of the elements rather than merely the overall performance [[25:168|AIH 8-10]].

quiz.q: What does the AIH call by far the most important flight instructor responsibility?
options: Keeping a current reference library
Professional appearance and habits
Pilot supervision of solo flight
Attending a FIRC every two years
quiz.why: Providing guidance and restraint with respect to learners' solo operations is by far the most important flight instructor responsibility [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. A library and appearance matter [[25:164|AIH 8-6]] [[25:167|AIH 8-9]], but the AIH does not rank them first.

quiz.q: Before you sign the practical test recommendation on the 8710-1, what should the applicant have demonstrated?
options: No less than the complete ACS/PTS procedure
Only the tasks missed on the knowledge test
Most tasks, with the rest briefed on the ground
Whatever the examiner says will be tested
quiz.why: The recommendation imposes a serious responsibility: the demonstration should in no instance be less than the complete procedure in the applicable ACS/PTS [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

quiz.q: Your instrument applicant will apply in September. Which months are the '2 calendar months preceding the month of application' in 61.39(a)(6)(i)?
options: June, July and August
Any day in the last 60 days
July and August
August only
quiz.why: 61.39(a)(6)(i) counts training received and logged within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application: for a September application, July and August [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)]] [[12:40|AC 61-65K A.1]]. The rule counts calendar months, not the 60 days the AIH gives for the 8710-1 signature and the logbook endorsement [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

quiz.q: A pilot's flight review was not satisfactory. What should go in the logbook?
options: 'Dual instruction given'
'Flight review failed' and the date
Nothing at all for that flight
An A.69 entry marked unsatisfactory
quiz.why: Log it as 'dual instruction given', not as a failure [[15:28|AC 61-98E 4.4.1]]; no entry showing unsatisfactory performance is required [[12:53|AC 61-65K A.69]]. You still sign the logbook of everyone you train [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189(a)]].

quiz.q: Who may give an IPC in a single-engine airplane, per AC 61-98E's instructor requirements?
options: Any CFI whose recent experience is current
A CFII with instrument ratings on both certificates
Any commercial pilot with an instrument rating
Only a designated pilot examiner or inspector
quiz.why: The instructor must hold an instrument rating on both the pilot certificate and the flight instructor certificate appropriate to the category and class [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]]. Examiners may also give IPCs, but so may authorized instructors [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(3)]].

quiz.q: A learner asks about a GPS mode you are not sure of. Which response shows sincerity?
options: Give your best guess with confidence
Change to a subject you know well
Say it won't be on the checkride
Say you're unsure; look it up together
quiz.why: Be straightforward and honest; hiding inadequacy behind a smokescreen of unrelated instruction costs respect [[25:166|AIH 8-8]]. If in doubt, admit it, because learners sense a bluff quickly [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

quiz.q: Your learner flew a fine ILS, you said nothing, and next lesson she seems flat. Which Figure 8-4 method did you skip?
options: Admit errors
Be consistent
Approach learners as individuals
Give credit when due
quiz.why: When learners do something extremely well and it goes unnoticed, they may become frustrated; deserved praise is usually ample reward and an incentive to do better [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your instrument learner is discouraged after three rough holding lessons. Following the AIH's advice for slow progress, what do you do next?
options: Keep flying full holds until they are right
Set easier goals, one element at a time
Tell him holds are easy for most
Skip holds and return to them after the checkride
final_quiz.why: For learners who show slow progress from discouragement, assign more easily attained goals: separate the task into elements, let the learner get good at each, and raise the difficulty as confidence grows [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies a perfect DME arc, but you suspect she has memorized it. How does the AIH suggest you check her understanding?
options: Ask her to fly the same arc twice more
Give her a written test on DME arcs
Watch her fly it again using the autopilot
Have her vary it or combine it with other tasks
final_quiz.why: When you suspect a maneuver is flown correctly without understanding, require the learner to vary it slightly, combine it with other operations or apply its elements to other maneuvers [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Besides why pilots train to standards and how the standards are set, what does the AIH say instructors should help pilots understand?
options: That meeting the standard gives a limited safety margin
That the examiner may relax a standard on a good day
That passing the checkride proves full proficiency
That the ACS limits are also the lesson goals
final_quiz.why: The AIH says it is important to provide an understanding of why pilots are trained to standards, how these standards are set, and that meeting the standard provides a limited margin of safety [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]. Lesson standards should reach or exceed the ACS/PTS, not stop at the test limits [[25:171|AIH 9-1]], and practical tests are only a sampling of pilot ability [[1:39|PHAK 1-24]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement matches the AIH on emphasizing the positive?
options: Learners must suffer a little to learn
Leave emergencies out of training
Failure often reflects the teaching
Praise should replace all criticism
final_quiz.why: A learner's failure to perform often results from the instructor's inability to transfer the information, and nothing in aviation demands that learners suffer. Emergencies are still taught, after normal operations [[25:161|AIH 8-3]], and errors still need constructive criticism [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your student pilot lands well when you talk her through it but needs help on about one landing in four. Is she ready to solo?
options: Yes, since most of her landings are fine
Not yet; she must be consistent unaided
Yes, if today's wind is light
Only with a radio talk-down on final
final_quiz.why: Solo readiness requires consistency in the solo tasks, performed without need of instructor assistance [[25:163|AIH 8-5]] and consistent ability on all fundamental maneuvers [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. Do not talk to a solo learner on short final [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: You carry a handheld radio for your learner's first solo. How does the AIH say to use it?
options: Few calls; none on short final
Talk her through each landing by radio
Leave it off so she feels truly alone
Call her only once she has landed
final_quiz.why: A radio lets you end the solo if you see a problem developing, but keep calls to a minimum and do not talk to the learner on short final [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Another instructor wants to send a learner to a stage check 'to see where she is'. What does the AIH say instructors should do first?
options: Let the check pilot set her goals
Skip the stage check if she is behind
Send her anyway so the check pilot can teach her
Verify she meets the proficiency requirements
final_quiz.why: Teaching instructors should verify that learners meet the proficiency requirements before sending them for any stage check [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Which three things does the 61.39(a)(6) practical test endorsement certify?
options: Medical, age and English proficiency
Recent training, readiness, missed areas reviewed
Total, cross-country and night flight time
Knowledge test score, aircraft and examiner
final_quiz.why: The instructor certifies training received and logged within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application, that the applicant is prepared, and satisfactory knowledge of the areas missed on the knowledge test [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)]].

final_quiz.q: Your instrument applicant's checkride is on May 20. Within what period must her 3 hours of instrument flight training in an airplane fall?
options: The 60 days after she applies
The 6 calendar months before May
2 calendar months before May 20
Any time since the knowledge test
final_quiz.why: The rule requires 3 hours of instrument flight training from an authorized instructor in an appropriate airplane within 2 calendar months before the date of the practical test [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]]. A.44 uses the same 'date of the test' wording [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.44]].

final_quiz.q: An endorsement you wrote uses different words from the AC 61-65K sample. Is it valid?
options: No, the AC 61-65K wording is mandatory
Only if an FAA inspector approves it first
Only for knowledge test endorsements, not others
Yes, if it cites the part 61 section
final_quiz.why: Endorsements need not be worded exactly as in the AC, but at a minimum the instructor must cite the part 61 section completed [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]; wording close to the AC is recommended [[25:202|AIH C-1]]. The AC itself is not legally binding in its own right [[12:4|AC 61-65K 1]].

final_quiz.q: Besides each person's name, what must your record of practical test endorsements show, and for how long?
options: Kind of test, date, result; 3 years
Date of the endorsement only; 1 year
The full training syllabus used; 5 years
Every lesson flown, until the next flight review
final_quiz.why: Record the name of each person endorsed for a knowledge or practical test, the kind of test, the date and the results, and keep the records for at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot wants a complex airplane endorsement, but after two flights his gear and propeller management are still weak. What does the AIH say to do?
options: Sign it; he will improve with use
Sign it with a written limitation
Debrief; schedule more training or refer
Tell him to go find an easier instructor elsewhere
final_quiz.why: If performance is insufficient for sign-off, debrief all problem areas and schedule further instruction, or refer the pilot to another instructor [[25:205|AIH C-4]]. The 61.31(e) endorsement certifies the pilot is proficient, so it cannot be signed yet [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(e)]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot asks for a flight review and an IPC in one session. You hold ASEL and instrument-airplane ratings on both certificates. What is true?
options: They must be done on separate days
Your IPC replaces the flight review
Only a DPE may combine the two
You may combine them at your discretion
final_quiz.why: The flight review may be accomplished in combination with 61.57 and other recent experience requirements at the instructor's discretion [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(h)]]. The 61.56(d) substitutes are proficiency checks or practical tests by an examiner, an approved check airman or the Armed Forces, and certain flight instructor practical tests; an IPC from a CFI is not among them [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)]].

final_quiz.q: Which behavior does the AIH list under demeanor as something to avoid?
options: Reacting differently to the same error
Admitting a mistake you made
Speaking positively, descriptively and normally
Accepting the learner's faults and problems
final_quiz.why: The successful instructor avoids reacting differently to similar or identical errors at different times [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]. Admitting errors and accepting the learner are recommended [[25:162|AIH 8-4]] [[25:166|AIH 8-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's approach scores have been flat for three lessons, and he says he may quit. What is the AIH's first line of defense?
options: Fly the same approach until it gets better
Explain learning rarely moves at a steady pace
Hide his scores so he stops worrying
Tell him others learned this faster
final_quiz.why: Learning plateaus are a common source of frustration; the first line of defense is to explain that learning seldom proceeds at a constant pace and that results will follow [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. Hiding progress breaks 'keep learners informed' [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

final_quiz.q: Which praise habit does the AIH warn against?
options: Praising one specific, well-flown maneuver
Praising progress before the critique
Praise given too freely
Praise that the learner has earned
final_quiz.why: Praise pays dividends when deserved, but when given too freely it becomes valueless [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Comments on progress before areas to improve are recommended [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

takeaways: This Task is tested whenever the FOI are: the PTS requires Tasks E, F and G.
Adequate instruction means analyzing each learner and changing methods to fit.
Train to the ACS/PTS but teach beyond it; it is a testing document, not a lesson plan.
Emphasize the positive: success first, emergencies after normal operations, progress before critique.
Supervision is the most important flight instructor duty: evaluate by elements, guard solo flight and the outside scan.
Sign a recommendation only after the complete ACS procedure; know 61.39(a)(6), A.42 to A.44 and the 3 hours in 2 calendar months.
For additional training, find what the rule requires, then what the pilot needs; never log a review or IPC as a failure.
Professional means sincere, accepting, neat, calm, clean-spoken and consistent, and admitting your own errors.
cfi_notes: PTS and 9B wording differ. The PTS says 'establishing standards of performance'; the AIH heading is 'Standards of Performance' and Figure 8-1 says 'Demanding appropriate standards of performance' [[25:159|AIH 8-1]] [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. The PTS puts minimizing frustration under professionalism, while the AIH teaches it as an aviation instructor responsibility [[25:162|AIH 8-4]] and also lists it among the Instructor Do's [[25:166|AIH 8-8]]. Recognize both.

Source conflict on the recommendation window: AIH 9-13 says the 8710-1 signature is valid for 60 days and should carry the same date as the logbook endorsement [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. 14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)(i) and AC 61-65K A.1 count training within 2 calendar months preceding the month of application [[60:219|14 CFR 61.39(a)(6)]] [[12:40|AC 61-65K A.1]]. Teach the rule's wording.

A.44, the instrument prerequisite endorsement, says training within 2 calendar months preceding the date of the test, while A.1 says the month of application [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.44]] [[12:40|AC 61-65K A.1]]. The instrument rule itself requires 3 hours of instrument flight training in an airplane within 2 calendar months before the date of the practical test [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)(i)]]. Plan the last lessons so both windows are met.

Who may give an IPC: AIH C-4 says aircraft and instrument ratings must be on the instructor certificate and cites 61.57(d)(2) [[25:205|AIH C-4]], but in the current rule (d)(2) covers where the IPC is flown and (d)(3) lists who may give it, including an authorized instructor [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(3)]]. AC 61-98E states the requirement plainly: instrument ratings on both the pilot and the instructor certificates [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]]. Quote the AC.

IPC devices: 14 CFR 61.57(d)(2) lists an aircraft, an FFS or an FTD for the IPC [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(2)]], and the FAA may approve other devices for specific purposes [[60:194|14 CFR 61.4(c)]]. AC 61-98E says only AATDs, not BATDs, may be used for the IPC and to check the device's LOA for its credit [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.2]]. Teach the AC's rule and check the LOA and the current ACS before planning ATD time.

Solo decision: AIH 8-5 calls it a joint decision between learner and instructor [[25:163|AIH 8-5]], while AIH 9-13 says the instructor is the only person in a position to determine solo readiness [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. They fit together: involve the learner, but the endorsement and its limits are yours alone [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(d)(1)]].

How it is tested: expect 'your learner ... what do you do?' questions, because the PTS asks evaluators to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions. The PTS also lists knowledge of the instructor's responsibilities for certification, logbook entries and endorsements among the satisfactory-performance items, so an examiner may hand you a logbook and ask for an endorsement.

Vocabulary: AIH Chapter 8 says 'evaluation of learner ability' [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]; Chapter 9 says 'assessment of piloting ability' and adds collaborative assessment [[25:181|AIH 9-11]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. The FOI lesson FOI.I.E covers assessment and critique in depth.

The CFI lessons FI.I.E (responsibilities and professionalism) and AI.II.K (endorsements) cover the CFI ACS versions of this material. The CFII-specific points here are 61.195(c), 61.65(d)(2), A.42 to A.44 and the IPC [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]] [[60:251|14 CFR 61.65(d)(2)]] [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]].
gaps: No source here says how many lessons or approaches make an instrument applicant 'consistent' enough for a recommendation; the AIH says only that the demonstration must be no less than the complete ACS/PTS procedure [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
The Instrument Rating ACS itself, including its IPC task table, is not one of the build sources. Read the current ACS for the exact IPC tasks [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.3]].
No source sets how long to keep a flight review or IPC plan of action; AC 61-98E says only 'for an appropriate period' [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3]] [[15:33|AC 61-98E 5.4.2]].
No source here defines 'appropriately dressed'; the AIH says only neat, clean and appropriate to professional status [[25:167|AIH 8-9]].
The PTS references FAA-H-8083-9; this lesson uses only the current 9B, so older-edition wording the 9B dropped is not covered.

activities.intro: Tap a statement, then the K1 responsibility it belongs to.

Change methods as the learner advances

Lesson standards reach the ACS before checkride prep

First lesson: an easy, normal flight to a nearby airport
